unit.name: Relational Databases and SQL
unit.subtitle: Designing relational tables and writing SQL to query, insert, update and delete data

lessons.title: Relational Databases: Tables, Keys and Relationships
lessons.description: Tables, records, fields, primary keys and foreign keys — why relations beat one big spreadsheet.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Database?

A database is an organised collection of data. Unlike a simple spreadsheet, a database is designed to store large amounts of information and allow it to be searched, sorted and updated quickly. Schools use databases to store pupil records; hospitals use them to track patient appointments; online shops use them to manage product stock. Anywhere large amounts of structured data need to be managed, a database is the tool of choice.

Relational Databases

A relational database stores data in multiple linked tables rather than one large list. Each table holds data about a single topic (for example, students, or courses). The tables are connected to each other using special key fields. This structure was developed to solve two serious problems that arise when you try to keep everything in one place: data redundancy and data inconsistency.

Key Fact

Data redundancy means storing the same piece of data in more than one place. Data inconsistency means different copies of the same data ending up with different values. Relational databases tackle both by storing each piece of data in exactly one place.

Tables, Records and Fields

Every relational database is made up of tables. Each table has a name (for example, Students) and is divided into columns called fields (or attributes) and rows called records (or tuples).

  • A field (also called an attribute) is a single category of data — for example, student_name or year_group. Each field has a specified data type: text, integer, date, Boolean and so on.
  • A record (also called a tuple or row) is one complete entry in the table — all the data about one particular student, for example.

Think of a table like a grid: the column headings are the fields, and each row is a record. Here is a sample Students table:

The Students table has four fields: student_id, student_name, year_group, tutor_group.

Sample records:

1 | Aisha Khan | 10 | 10A
2 | Ben Okafor | 11 | 11B
3 | Chloe Davis | 10 | 10A

Here student_id is the primary key — each student has a unique number that is never repeated or reused. The other fields store descriptive information about the student. Notice that 10A appears twice: this is fine because it is just a tutor group label, not the student’s main identifier.

Primary Keys

Every table must have a primary key. This is a field whose value is different for every record, so it can be used to pinpoint exactly one row. In the Students table, student_id is the primary key. You cannot use student_name as a primary key because two students could share the same name.

Primary keys are often auto-generated integers (1, 2, 3…) although they can be any unique value — an NHS number, a National Insurance number, a barcode. The key point is that no two records can ever have the same primary key value, and the field must always have a value (it cannot be left blank).

Foreign Keys

A second table—say, an Enrolments table—needs to know which student each enrolment belongs to. Rather than copy the student’s full name and year group into the Enrolments table (which would create redundancy), we store only the student’s student_id. In the Enrolments table, this field is called a foreign key.

The foreign key “points to” the primary key in the other table. This is how the two tables are linked. If you want to find a student’s name for a given enrolment, you look up the student_id in the Students table using the foreign key as a reference.

We have two tables:

Students (student_id [PK], student_name, year_group)
Courses (course_id [PK], course_title)
Enrolments (enrolment_id [PK], student_id [FK], course_id [FK])

The Enrolments table uses student_id as a foreign key linking back to Students, and course_id as a foreign key linking back to Courses. This means:

  • Aisha’s name is stored once in Students — there is no need to write “Aisha Khan” in every enrolment row for her.
  • If Aisha’s name is ever corrected, you update it in one place and it is immediately correct everywhere — no inconsistency possible.

Relationships Between Tables

The most common relationship at GCSE is a one-to-many relationship. In our example, one student can have many enrolments, but each enrolment belongs to exactly one student. The foreign key always sits in the “many” side of the relationship (the Enrolments table), pointing back to the primary key on the “one” side (the Students table).

Key Fact

A primary key uniquely identifies a record in its own table. A foreign key in one table references the primary key in another table, linking the two tables together. In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key is always in the “many” table.

Why Not Just Use One Big Table?

Imagine trying to store all student and course information in a single flat table with columns like: student_id, student_name, year_group, course_title, teacher_name, room_number. Every time a student takes two courses, you would need two rows — with the student’s name and year group repeated in both. This is data redundancy. Now imagine the student changes year group: you would need to update every row for that student. Miss one, and you now have inconsistent data. The relational approach solves both problems by splitting data across properly linked tables.

Vocabulary Equivalence Note

The same concepts appear with different names depending on context. When discussing an abstract data model: an entity maps to a table; an attribute maps to a field; an entity identifier maps to a primary key. Your exam may use either set of terms — you need to recognise both.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to “define primary key” or “explain the purpose of a foreign key”, be precise: a primary key uniquely identifies a record (not just “identifies”) and a foreign key references the primary key in another table (not just “links tables”). For a 4-mark explain question, name the key concept, say what it does, explain the benefit (e.g. eliminates redundancy), and give an example from the scenario in the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A relational database stores data in linked tables, each containing records (rows) and fields (columns). Primary keys uniquely identify each record; foreign keys link one table to another.
  • Data redundancy (repeated data) and data inconsistency (conflicting copies) are the two core problems that relational databases solve by storing each piece of data in exactly one place.
  • The terms entity, attribute and entity identifier are abstract equivalents of table, field and primary key — you need to recognise both sets.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by a primary key in a relational database?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A field (or combination of fields) that uniquely identifies each record in a table; no two records can share the same primary key value and it cannot be empty. Secure: A field that uniquely identifies a record / ensures every row is different. Developing: A field used to identify records (partial — doesn't stress uniqueness or no-null rule). Emerging: A key in a table (vague, insufficient).

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by data redundancy and describe one problem it causes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Data redundancy is the unnecessary repetition of the same data in multiple places (1); storing a student's name in both the Students table and the Enrolments table is an example (1); if the name needs to change, every copy must be updated (1); missing any copy leads to data inconsistency, where different records show different values for the same fact (1). Secure: Defines redundancy correctly and identifies one clear problem. Developing: Identifies redundancy as repeated data but problem explanation is vague. Emerging: Repeating data named; no consequence explained.

practice_questions.text: A school database has a Students table and an Enrolments table. The Students table contains the field student_id as a primary key. State the name given to the field student_id when it appears in the Enrolments table, and explain its purpose.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The field is a foreign key (1); it references the primary key in the Students table (1); this creates a link between the two tables (1); allowing enrolment rows to be associated with the correct student without repeating all the student's details (1). Secure: Names foreign key and explains that it links to the Students table. Developing: Names foreign key but purpose is vague. Emerging: Names it a key but doesn't use the correct term.

practice_questions.text: A database designer is considering whether to store all student and course information in a single flat table or to use a relational database with separate linked tables. Compare these two approaches, referring to data redundancy and data inconsistency.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Flat table requires repeating student details for every course they take (redundancy) whereas a relational database stores student details once, referenced by a foreign key (no redundancy); flat table risks inconsistency if one copy of a student's name is updated but another is not, whereas a relational database updates the single source record so inconsistency cannot occur; relational database requires more complex design but scales better for large datasets. Secure: Identifies redundancy and inconsistency differences with clear comparison language. Developing: Identifies problems with flat tables but comparison is one-sided. Emerging: Mentions redundancy or inconsistency but no direct comparison.

practice_questions.text: Identify the data type most appropriate for the field year_group in a Students table if it stores values such as 10, 11.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Integer (accept whole number). Developing: Number (accept if context makes integer clear). Emerging: Any other data type.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a one-to-many relationship in a relational database and give an example using Students and Courses tables.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: One record in the first table can be associated with many records in the second table, but each record in the second table is associated with only one record in the first (1); example: one student can be enrolled on many courses (1); each enrolment record belongs to exactly one student (1); the foreign key (student_id) sits in the Enrolments/many-side table (1). Secure: Correct definition with a clear example. Developing: Example given without precise definition of the relationship. Emerging: Mentions one table having more records than another — vague.

glossary_terms.definition: An organised collection of data stored and accessed electronically, designed for efficient retrieval and management.
A type of database that organises data into two or more linked tables, removing repeated data and connecting information through key fields.
The unnecessary repetition of the same data in multiple places within a database, which wastes storage and makes updates harder.
A problem that occurs when copies of the same data in different places go out of step with each other, showing different values for the same fact.
A structured grid in a database that stores data about one topic, made up of rows and columns.
A single row in a database table, representing one complete set of information about one item or person.
A field (or combination of fields) in a database table that uniquely identifies each record; no two records can share the same value and it cannot be empty.
A field in one table that references the primary key in another table, creating a link between the two tables.

lessons.title: SQL: Retrieving Data with SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY
lessons.description: Writing SQL queries to retrieve data, filter with WHERE conditions and sort results with ORDER BY.
lessons.content_html:
What Is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to communicate with a relational database. When a website shows you a list of products, when a teacher pulls up your grades, or when a bank checks your balance, SQL is running behind the scenes. In this lesson, we focus on retrieving data — asking the database to show us records that match certain criteria.

We will use the same three tables introduced in the previous lesson throughout all our examples:

  • Students — student_id (PK), student_name, year_group
  • Courses — course_id (PK), course_title
  • Enrolments — enrolment_id (PK), student_id (FK), course_id (FK)

SELECT and FROM

Every retrieval query begins with SELECT, followed by the column names you want to see. Then comes FROM, followed by the table name. If you want all columns, use a star (*) instead of listing them.

Query: Show all data from the Students table.

SELECT *
FROM Students;

The * means “all columns”. The database returns every row and every field from the Students table. The semicolon marks the end of the query.

Query: Show only the student_name column from the Students table.

SELECT student_name
FROM Students;

This time only one column is returned. You can list multiple columns separated by commas: SELECT student_name, year_group FROM Students;

Filtering with WHERE

Most of the time you don’t want every row — you want rows that meet a condition. The WHERE clause lets you set that condition. The database checks each row and only includes it in the results if the condition is true.

You can use these comparison operators in a WHERE clause: = (equal), <> (not equal), < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal to), >= (greater than or equal to). You can also combine conditions with AND and OR, and use LIKE with a % wildcard for partial text matches.

Equal to (text value):

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE student_name = ‘Aisha Khan’;

Text values are wrapped in single quotes. This returns only the row where the student’s name is exactly ‘Aisha Khan’.

Greater than (numeric value):

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE year_group > 10;

Returns only students in year 11 (or above, if higher year groups exist). Numbers do not need quotes.

Combining conditions with AND:

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE year_group = 10 AND student_name LIKE ‘A%’;

Both conditions must be true. LIKE ‘A%’ matches any name that starts with the letter A. The % is a wildcard meaning “any characters here”.

Either condition with OR:

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE year_group = 10 OR year_group = 11;

Returns students in year 10 OR year 11 — either condition being true is enough to include the row.

Key Fact

In a WHERE clause: text values go inside single quotes; numbers do not. The wildcard character % is used with LIKE: LIKE ‘%son’ matches anything ending in ‘son’; LIKE ‘A%’ matches anything starting with ‘A’; LIKE ‘%art%’ matches anything containing ‘art’.

Sorting with ORDER BY

By default, rows come back in no guaranteed order. To sort the results, add an ORDER BY clause at the end of the query, followed by the column name. Use ASC for ascending order (A to Z, lowest to highest) or DESC for descending order (Z to A, highest to lowest). If you leave out ASC or DESC, the database defaults to ascending.

Alphabetical order:

SELECT student_name
FROM Students
ORDER BY student_name ASC;

Returns all student names sorted A to Z.

Filtered and sorted together:

SELECT student_name, year_group
FROM Students
WHERE year_group = 10
ORDER BY student_name DESC;

Returns only year 10 students, but sorted Z to A by name. Notice the clause order: SELECT — FROM — WHERE — ORDER BY. This order is fixed and must not be changed.

Querying Across Two Tables

Exam questions may ask you to retrieve data from two tables at once. You can do this by listing both tables after FROM and adding a WHERE condition that matches the primary key in one table to the foreign key in the other. This effectively joins the tables by finding rows where the key values match.

Task: Find the names of all students enrolled on course number 3.

SELECT Students.student_name
FROM Students, Enrolments
WHERE Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id
AND Enrolments.course_id = 3;

Step by step: FROM Students, Enrolments tells the database to look at both tables. WHERE Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id links the two tables through matching key values (primary key = foreign key). The second AND condition filters to course 3 only. You can use TableName.ColumnName notation when the same column name appears in both tables, to avoid ambiguity.

Key Fact

The four retrieval keywords must appear in this order: SELECT (what columns) → FROM (which table or tables) → WHERE (which rows, optional) → ORDER BY (what sort order, optional). Swapping the order causes a syntax error.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In a 5-mark SQL question, examiners typically award one mark each for: correct SELECT with named columns, correct FROM with correct table(s), correct WHERE condition, correct comparison operator, and correct ORDER BY. Common errors: forgetting single quotes around text values; using = instead of LIKE for wildcard matching; putting ORDER BY before WHERE; writing a column name that doesn’t exist in the given table. Always re-read the table schema in the question before writing your query.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • SELECT names the columns you want; FROM names the table. Use * for all columns. Clause order is fixed: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → ORDER BY.
  • WHERE filters rows using comparison operators (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=), combined with AND/OR, or LIKE with % for partial text matches. Text values need single quotes; numbers do not.
  • ORDER BY sorts results ASC (ascending) or DESC (descending). To query two tables, list both in FROM and use a WHERE condition that matches the primary key to the foreign key.

practice_questions.text: Write an SQL query to retrieve the student_name and year_group of all students from a table called Students.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: SELECT student_name, year_group FROM Students; — all five marks (SELECT correct columns (1), FROM correct table (1), no spurious WHERE (1), syntactically correct (1), semicolon / overall structure (1)). Secure: SELECT and FROM correct, minor syntax issue. Developing: SELECT present, wrong column names or table name. Emerging: SQL attempted but fundamentally incorrect structure.

practice_questions.text: Write an SQL query to find the student_name of every student in year group 10, sorted in descending alphabetical order by student_name.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: SELECT student_name FROM Students WHERE year_group = 10 ORDER BY student_name DESC; — SELECT (1), FROM (1), WHERE year_group = 10 (1), ORDER BY student_name (1), DESC (1). Secure: All clauses present, minor error in one (e.g. quotes around 10). Developing: WHERE and ORDER BY present but one clause wrong. Emerging: Only SELECT/FROM correct.

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of the WHERE clause in an SQL SELECT query.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: WHERE filters rows, returning only those where the specified condition is true, so the query results contain only relevant records. Secure: WHERE filters results to rows matching a condition. Developing: WHERE selects certain rows (vague about condition). Emerging: It's part of the query (no explanation of filtering).

practice_questions.text: State the difference between using AND and OR to combine conditions in a WHERE clause.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: AND requires both conditions to be true for a row to be included; OR requires only one of the conditions to be true. Secure: AND = both true, OR = at least one true. Developing: AND is stricter / OR gives more results (partially correct, no precision). Emerging: One named but not distinguished from the other.

practice_questions.text: Write an SQL query to find the student_name of all students whose name contains the letters 'son', from a table called Students.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: SELECT student_name FROM Students WHERE student_name LIKE '%son%'; — SELECT (1), FROM Students (1), WHERE (1), LIKE (1), '%son%' with correct wildcard placement (1). Secure: LIKE used correctly but wildcard position wrong (e.g. 'son%'). Developing: WHERE present but = used instead of LIKE. Emerging: Query attempted, no LIKE or wildcard.

Mastering: The Students table is not included — student_name is in Students, not Enrolments (1); both tables must be listed in FROM (1); a WHERE condition must link Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id (1); corrected: SELECT Students.student_name FROM Students, Enrolments WHERE Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id AND Enrolments.course_id = 5; (1). Secure: Identifies the missing table and writes a working two-table query. Developing: Identifies the problem but correction is incomplete. Emerging: Notes something is wrong but no clear fix.

glossary_terms.definition: Structured Query Language — a standard language used to create, retrieve, update and delete data in a relational database.
The SQL keyword that specifies which columns should be shown in the results of a query.
The SQL keyword that names the table (or tables) from which data should be retrieved.
The SQL keyword that filters rows, returning only those where the specified condition is true.
The SQL clause that sorts the results of a query in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order based on one or more columns.

lessons.title: SQL: Modifying Data with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
lessons.description: Using INSERT INTO to add rows, UPDATE SET to modify data, and DELETE FROM with a safe WHERE clause.
lessons.content_html:
Modifying a Database

So far you have learnt to retrieve data with SELECT. Real databases also need to grow and change: new students join a school and need rows adding; contact details change and need updating; leavers’ records are eventually removed. SQL provides three commands for these operations: INSERT INTO, UPDATE, and DELETE FROM. We use the same Students, Courses and Enrolments tables as before throughout all the examples in this lesson.

Reminder of the schema:
Students — student_id (PK), student_name, year_group
Courses — course_id (PK), course_title
Enrolments — enrolment_id (PK), student_id (FK), course_id (FK)

INSERT INTO — Adding New Rows

To add a new record, use:

INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, …)
VALUES (value1, value2, …);

The columns list and the values list must match in number and order. Text values go in single quotes; integers do not. You do not have to include every column — you can omit columns that have a default value or are auto-generated by the database (such as an auto-increment primary key).

Task: Add a new student, Dani Osei, in year group 10, with student_id 4.

INSERT INTO Students (student_id, student_name, year_group)
VALUES (4, ‘Dani Osei’, 10);

After this query runs, the Students table gains a new row: 4 | Dani Osei | 10. Notice that 4 (an integer) has no quotes, while ‘Dani Osei’ (text) does.

Adding an enrolment record: To enrol Dani (student_id = 4) on course 2:

INSERT INTO Enrolments (enrolment_id, student_id, course_id)
VALUES (10, 4, 2);

All three values are integers so none need quotes. The foreign key value (student_id = 4) must already exist in the Students table — you cannot enrol a student who doesn’t exist.

UPDATE — Changing Existing Data

To change data in existing rows, use:

UPDATE table_name
SET column1 = value1, column2 = value2, …
WHERE condition;

The SET clause names the columns to change and their new values. The WHERE clause identifies which rows to update. You can update more than one column at once by separating them with commas in the SET clause.

Task: Change Aisha Khan’s year group to 11.

UPDATE Students
SET year_group = 11
WHERE student_name = ‘Aisha Khan’;

Only the row (or rows) where student_name equals ‘Aisha Khan’ is changed. All other rows remain exactly as they were.

Updating two columns at once: Rename student_id 2 and move them to year 11.

UPDATE Students
SET student_name = ‘Benjamin Okafor’, year_group = 11
WHERE student_id = 2;

Two columns are updated in a single query. Using student_id in the WHERE clause is safer than using student_name, because student_id is the primary key and uniquely identifies one row.

Key Fact

Critical rule: An UPDATE without a WHERE clause changes every single row in the table. Writing UPDATE Students SET year_group = 11; would change all students’ year groups to 11, overwriting all existing data. Always include a WHERE clause to target only the intended rows.

DELETE FROM — Removing Rows

To remove one or more rows from a table, use:

DELETE FROM table_name
WHERE condition;

The WHERE clause identifies which rows to remove. Every row matching the condition is permanently deleted — this cannot be undone in a basic SQL query. If no WHERE clause is given, every row in the table is deleted.

Task: Remove the student with student_id 3 from the Students table.

DELETE FROM Students
WHERE student_id = 3;

Only the row where student_id = 3 is deleted. Using the primary key in the WHERE clause ensures exactly one row is targeted.

Deleting an enrolment: Remove all enrolments for student_id 1.

DELETE FROM Enrolments
WHERE student_id = 1;

If student 1 has three enrolment records, all three are deleted by this single query because all three rows satisfy the condition.

Key Fact

The WHERE clause on DELETE is never optional in practice. DELETE FROM Students; without a WHERE clause deletes every student record in the table — all data is lost. Always test a WHERE condition with a SELECT query first to confirm it targets the right rows, before running DELETE.

Test Before You Modify

A good habit before running any UPDATE or DELETE on a real database is to first run a SELECT query with the same WHERE condition. If the SELECT returns exactly the rows you expected, you can be confident the UPDATE or DELETE will target the right records and no others. For example, before running DELETE FROM Students WHERE year_group = 10; first run SELECT * FROM Students WHERE year_group = 10; to review exactly which rows will be affected. This test-first approach is a practical way to prevent accidental data loss.

Comparing the Three Commands

To summarise the three data-modification commands:

  • INSERT INTO — adds one new row. Needs column names and matching values. Cannot target existing rows.
  • UPDATE…SET…WHERE — changes values in existing rows. Must use WHERE to target specific rows. Can update multiple columns in one query.
  • DELETE FROM…WHERE — removes whole rows. Must use WHERE to target specific rows. The deletion is immediate and permanent.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error in SQL modification questions is writing an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause. Examiners will penalise this directly — and in some mark schemes, omitting WHERE on a DELETE question loses all marks because the command would wipe the entire table. For INSERT INTO, remember: the column list and value list must have the same number of items and be in the same order. If the question gives you a table schema, check the column names and data types before writing your answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • INSERT INTO adds a new row: list column names, then matching values. Text values need single quotes; integers do not.
  • UPDATE changes existing rows: SET names the columns and new values, WHERE targets which rows. Without WHERE, every row is changed.
  • DELETE FROM removes rows: WHERE targets which rows. Without WHERE, every row is deleted. Always include WHERE — this is a non-negotiable safety rule.

practice_questions.text: Write an SQL query to add a new student with student_id 5, student_name 'Ellie Marsh', and year_group 11 into a table called Students.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: INSERT INTO Students (student_id, student_name, year_group) VALUES (5, 'Ellie Marsh', 11); — INSERT INTO Students (1), correct column list (1), VALUES keyword (1), correct values with 'Ellie Marsh' in quotes and integers without (1), syntactically correct / semicolon (1). Secure: All elements present, minor syntax error. Developing: INSERT INTO present and most values correct, column list missing or wrong. Emerging: INSERT attempted but fundamentally incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Write an SQL query to change the year_group to 11 for the student with student_id 3 in a table called Students.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: UPDATE Students SET year_group = 11 WHERE student_id = 3; — UPDATE Students (1), SET year_group = 11 (1), WHERE (1), student_id = 3 (1), overall syntax (1). Secure: Correct structure, minor error. Developing: UPDATE and SET present, WHERE missing or wrong condition. Emerging: Only UPDATE or SET present.

practice_questions.text:
A student writes: DELETE FROM Students;

Explain what this query will do and describe the change needed to make it safe.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The query deletes every row in the Students table because there is no WHERE clause (1); this means all student records are permanently removed (1); a WHERE clause is needed to target only the intended row(s) (1); for example: DELETE FROM Students WHERE student_id = 3; would delete only the student with id 3 (1). Secure: Identifies all-rows deletion problem and gives a correct fix. Developing: Identifies the problem but fix is vague. Emerging: Notes something is wrong without identifying the missing WHERE.

practice_questions.text: Write an SQL query to delete all enrolment records from a table called Enrolments where the course_id is 7.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: DELETE FROM Enrolments WHERE course_id = 7; — DELETE FROM Enrolments (1), WHERE (1), course_id = 7 (1), no quotes on integer (1), overall syntax (1). Secure: Correct query, minor issue. Developing: DELETE FROM correct, condition wrong (e.g. quotes around 7). Emerging: Only DELETE FROM Enrolments present.

practice_questions.text: State one difference between the INSERT INTO command and the UPDATE command in SQL.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: INSERT INTO adds a new row that did not previously exist, whereas UPDATE changes the values in one or more rows that already exist in the table. Secure: INSERT adds new row, UPDATE changes existing row. Developing: INSERT is for new data, UPDATE for old data (acceptable if sense is clear). Emerging: Lists both commands without stating a difference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why using the primary key in the WHERE clause of an UPDATE or DELETE query is considered best practice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The primary key uniquely identifies a single row (1); using it in WHERE guarantees that only one specific row is targeted (1); using a non-unique field (e.g. year_group) could accidentally match multiple rows (1); this would change or delete more records than intended, potentially causing data loss (1). Secure: Uniqueness point made clearly with consequence. Developing: Primary key is unique — one row targeted (partial, no consequence). Emerging: Primary key mentioned with no explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: What happens if you write UPDATE Students SET year_group = 12 without a WHERE clause?
options: Every row in the Students table has year_group changed to 12
